Field surveys of Tor putitora in the Himalayan foothills have documented that females attain sexual maturity when they reach a total length of approximately 33 cm [Lp = approximately 33 cm], a size typically achieved after several years of growth in productive riverine habitats. The corresponding wet weight at this developmental milestone is around 335 grams [Wwp = around 335 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to large sample populations from the Karnali River system. This species exhibits a remarkable ultimate size, with maximum recorded total lengths reaching 183 cm [Li = 183 cm], although some ichthyological databases list specimens attaining total lengths as great as 275 cm. The enormous adult body mass that accompanies such lengths, estimated at approximately 57,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 57,000 grams] based on allometric scaling relationships, positions the mahseer as one of the largest freshwater cyprinids in South Asia. These impressive dimensions are thought to be linked to its potamodromous life history, which allows individuals to exploit abundant food resources across expansive river stretches.

During controlled hatchery experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the incubation period for Tor putitora eggs was precisely recorded, with embryos hatching after approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days]. The tiny prolarvae that emerge from these incubating eggs possess a wet weight of merely 0.006 grams [Wwb = 0.006 grams], a value consistent with the species' relatively small egg diameter of 2 to 2.5 millimeters. This minute birth mass places the species among the more fecund large-bodied cyprinids, as the energetic investment per offspring is low, allowing females to produce thousands of eggs during each spawning event. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatching, gradually transitioning to exogenous feeding as the mouth opens and the yolk is resorbed. These early life stages experience intense mortality in the wild, but under the stable thermal regime maintained in captivity, the initial growth trajectory is remarkably consistent across broods.

Comparative studies of reproductive biology among South Asian cyprinids reveal that the total length at puberty for Tor putitora females, measured at 33 cm [Lp = 33 cm], is notably larger than that of many sympatric barb species, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth before the onset of gonadal maturation. The wet weight at puberty, standing at 335 grams [Wwp = 335 grams], similarly underscores this delayed reproductive schedule, which is thought to be an adaptation to unpredictable monsoon-driven flow regimes where early spawning success is highly variable. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight of the species, reaching as high as 57,000 grams [Wwi = 57,000 grams], represents an extreme endpoint of this delayed maturation strategy, allowing fully grown adults to dominate the highest trophic positions within their riverine ecosystems. Such large individuals, achieving total lengths of 183 cm [Li = 183 cm], are now increasingly rare due to overfishing and habitat fragmentation, but they remain a key target for conservation reintroduction programs.

Long-term mark-recapture studies conducted in the Kosi River system, coupled with otolith microchemistry analyses, have allowed researchers to estimate the maximum lifespan of Tor putitora under natural conditions. Individuals maintained in captivity at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] have been documented to survive for up to 10 years [am = up to 10 years], a longevity that is exceptional among large cyprinids and consistent with the species' slow pace of life. This extended lifespan, combined with the age at hatching of approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days] under those same thermal conditions, illustrates a life cycle that encompasses both a brief, vulnerable embryonic stage and a prolonged adult phase of repeated reproduction. The remarkable length of the adult stage provides multiple opportunities for iteroparous spawning, which buffers against occasional recruitment failures that are common in monsoonal rivers. Senescent individuals over a decade old are rarely captured in the wild, suggesting that natural mortality becomes concentrated in the oldest age classes.

Growth performance and metabolic scaling in Tor putitora have been investigated through respirometry trials and long-term pond culture experiments. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a cubic allometry, such that an individual of the ultimate total length of 183 cm [Li = 183 cm] achieves an asymptotic wet body mass of roughly 57,000 grams [Wwi = roughly 57,000 grams], while a female at the onset of puberty, measuring 33 cm [Lp = 33 cm] in total length, reaches a corresponding mass of 335 grams [Wwp = 335 grams]. These allometric coefficients are consistent with those reported for other large-bodied cyprinids, suggesting a conserved scaling of body shape. The neonatal wet weight of 0.006 grams [Wwb = 0.006 grams] at hatching, when contrasted with the adult mass, reveals a staggering four-orders-of-magnitude increase over the species' lifespan, a growth trajectory made possible by its powerful digestive physiology and high ingestion rates. Under optimal thermal conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum recorded longevity of 10 years [am = 10 years] provides ample time for this massive ontogenetic transformation to unfold.
